summary: VitalOrbit is a crew health co-pilot that helps astronauts monitor, evaluate and act on their own health during long-duration missions. We built an interactive prototype that learns each astronaut’s personal baseline and tracks sustained drift in 11 signals, including temperature, heart rate and variability, exercise, grip strength, mood, sleep, reaction time and radiation dose. Cross-signal rules turn them into clear Stable, Watch or Act statuses for immune, cardiovascular, bone and muscle, behavioral and radiation health. Every alert explains which signals changed and what to do next, and a ground-link module queues a summary when communication is delayed. NASA data is central: its radiation limits, bone-loss findings, cardiovascular research, and the OSDR and DONKI datasets shape the thresholds, schedules and planned data sources. On missions beyond low Earth orbit, help from Earth can be minutes away, so early, explainable warnings help crews catch small problems before they grow.
details:
What it does and how it works: VitalOrbit is a crew health co-pilot for long-duration missions. It learns each astronaut’s own baseline from the first 14 days, then tracks sustained drift in 11 signals (temperature, symptoms, heart rate, heart-rate variability, exercise, grip strength, back pain, mood, sleep, reaction time, radiation dose). Cross-signal rules turn them into five statuses (immune, cardiovascular, bone and muscle, behavioral, radiation), each shown as Stable, Watch or Act. Every alert explains which signals changed and what to do next, and a ground-link module queues a summary when communication is delayed.

Benefits and impact: On missions beyond low Earth orbit, radio delay to Mars can reach about 22 minutes each way, so astronauts must catch early changes themselves. VitalOrbit gives them an early, explained warning and a private, offline-first record. The same approach can support remote clinics and polar stations on Earth.

NASA data: The app uses NASA’s 600 mSv career radiation limit and 250 mSv solar particle event limit. It uses NASA’s reported bone loss of up to 1–2% per month. It schedules a jugular vein self-scan around flight day 50, based on NASA’s finding of abnormal flow in 6 of 11 crew. The plan connects NASA OSDR Inspiration4 datasets and the NASA DONKI space weather API.

Tools: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript and inline SVG, with Google Fonts. It runs in any web browser on simulated crew data and needs no special hardware. [Add any AI assistance your team used, if the rules ask for it.]

Creativity: Personal baselines instead of population averages, an “illness signature” across five signals, mission-day-aware checks, a built-in reaction test, and fully explainable alerts.

Team considerations: Safety (decision support only), privacy (data stays on board), low crew workload, and false alarms. A synthetic test on 120 simulated crews gave about 0.07 false alerts per mission and caught every seeded event. This is not clinical validation, so the next step is to replay the engine on NASA OSDR and analog-mission data.
